opening.headline: When tuning becomes worse, we will look into the order and criteria for determining whether the cause is data or method.
body: I've finished tuning with hundreds of examples, but if the answers are shakier than the basic model for some inputs, where should I start? If training was completed without errors and the settings were default, the next suspect is often the data, not the hyperparameters or method.

In this class, we will examine data problems by dividing them into label mismatch, distribution bias, duplication, leakage, lack of evidence, and format mismatch. Next, the instructor explains the data audit process, cases where data was improved by organizing it rather than increasing it, and cases where the method was changed because organizing the data did not solve the problem.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Data quality issues can be categorized into inconsistencies, biases, and leaks.
You can distinguish between data problems and method problems.

screens.title: I tuned it, but it got worse.
screens.lead: Read about a team whose results were different from expectations after tuning. It is helpful to read while thinking about what the possible causes might be.

visual.alt: An illustration showing three possible causes: data, hyperparameters, and methods when performance deteriorates after tuning.
labels: After tuning, the answer is shakier than the base model for some inputs

paragraphs: A team tuned a customer inquiry classification model. We trained with hundreds of examples, and the training was completed without any problems and there were no error messages. However, in some inputs, the answer is more shaky than the basic model.

There are three candidate causes. Maybe your training setup wasn't right, maybe you picked the wrong method for the task, or maybe there's a problem with the data itself. Settings can be measured by the learning curve and methods can be gauged by the nature of the work, but data issues are less obvious.

So the order of inspection is important. It is efficient to first question the data when the tuning results do not meet expectations, and then question the method when the solution is not resolved even after organizing the data. This class explains the sequence with evidence for each step.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The model learns the given examples as is. If there are flaws in the example, the model faithfully learns even those flaws.

screens.outro: First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Think back: An experience where tuning results were different from expectations
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about your own experience first and then click on it.

items.prompt: How many people created the labels for tuning data?
items.answer: For data created by multiple people, the degree of agreement between people often sets an upper limit on model performance. For example, in a text extraction task, if the passages people extracted matched only 70% of the time, it would be difficult for the model to be any better than that.

items.prompt: How much of your data were rejection responses or specific types?
items.answer: If the response rate in the training data is significantly different from the operationally desired rate, the model learns that rate as is. If you train with data that has too many rejection responses, your operations will also reject too often.

items.prompt: Did the training examples contain all the information on which to base your response?
items.answer: If the user's characteristics are mentioned in the response but the input does not contain such information, the model can learn to make up information without evidence. It is important to ensure that your input has all the information needed to respond.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's first look at the impact of mismatched labels.

screens.title: How label mismatch affects learning
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to see how mismatched and matched labeling makes a difference in training.

states.label: Data with mixed labels
states.body:
Let's say that the same type of input is labeled "Resolved" by Author A and "Requires further confirmation" by Author B. The model learns two correct answers simultaneously and becomes unstable about which one it will follow. It may seem that the same input produces different answers from day to day.

If multiple people created the data, agreement and consistency between authors will limit model performance. If people only matched 70% of the time, it's hard to expect the model to do much more than that. This issue is often hidden from the learning curve and only becomes apparent after seeing the results.

states.label: Data with unified standards
states.body:
If you create a label rubric and have the author judge by the same rules, the same type will be given the same label. The model learns consistent rules, so the results are stable. It's a good idea to include in your rubric how you judge borderline cases.

There are two ways to check: This involves double labeling, where two people separately label the same input, collect discrepancies to reinforce the standard, and check the standard itself. Increasing label agreement first is often more effective than collecting more data. After fixing the labels, compare them again with the same evaluation criteria as the previous training results to see if consistency has actually improved. The rubric is also a safeguard to help ensure that new writers make the same decisions when they come on board. Your judgment will be better if you write down borderline cases with examples.

screens.outro: In addition to labels, there are problems that arise from the organization of the entire data. Let's continue on the next screen.

screens.title: Distribution bias, duplication, leaks, lack of evidence
screens.lead: If you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, a short explanation and example will appear. Check them out one by one.

data.text: Data issues can be broadly categorized into six types. The first is distribution bias: if the distribution of example types in training data differs from that in operational inputs, the model learns this imbalance directly. The second is duplicate: when the same examples are repeated, specific patterns may lead to overfitting. The third is water leak: if evaluation data is mixed into training, performance metrics may appear artificially improved. The fourth is no basis: if information used in responses is not present in the inputs, the model learns to fabricate answers. The fifth is label inconsistency: assigning different answer labels to the same input creates conflicting learning objectives. The sixth is format mismatch: if the format during training differs from that during inference, performance degrades. None of these issues can be resolved by adjusting model settings alone—they must be addressed by modifying the data. Even when symptoms appear similar, the underlying causes may differ; thus, distinguishing the specific signals associated with each type enables faster diagnosis.

terms.tip: For example, if 60% of responses are "can't answer" but in production that should be around 5%, your model will reject excessively.
The same or almost the same examples are repeated. When certain patterns are overtrained and the same examples are used for verification, the metrics are also inflated.
This is a phenomenon where evaluation data is mixed with learning data. Because the model is hitting problems it has already seen, the metrics look better than they actually are.
For example, if the response praises a personal characteristic of the user, but that characteristic is not present in the input, the model can learn to invent the information.
The prompt and output format of the training example are different from those of the actual inference. If you unify them in the same format, the effect will be greater.

screens.outro: Now that you know the six types, let's look at a data audit, a process for systematically finding them.

screens.title: Data Audit and Distinguishing Data Issues vs. Method Issues
screens.lead: Click the Next button to follow the data audit process and subsequent judgment step by step.

steps.title: 1 Take a sample
steps.body: Since we cannot read the entire data, we take a sample and read it ourselves. You should select evenly by type to avoid a one-sided impression. If there is an input type that the model is currently wrong with, first check for an example of that type.

steps.title: 2 Check label matching
steps.body: Ensures that inputs of the same type are labeled the same. Comparing pieces created by different authors reveals points where standards diverge.

steps.title: 3 Aggregate the distribution
steps.body: Count the ratio of labels, response types, and input types. And compare whether that ratio is similar to the distribution desired for the operation. First, look to see if one response is too many.

steps.title: 4 Check for duplication and leaks
steps.body: Find identical or nearly identical examples and ensure that the same source material is included between training and validation. This step sometimes explains why the validation index is high.

steps.title: 5 Unify the format
steps.body: Make sure that all examples are in the same format as the actual inference. Prompts to be used for learning are also included in all examples. During this process, we check whether the information required for the response is in the input and whether there are any grammar or logic problems in the response.

steps.title: 6 Make up for remaining weaknesses
steps.body: If, after summarizing, there are still areas where the model is weak, add examples that directly target those areas. If there is still no change in the 50 or so good examples, look at the task definition or prompt again before increasing the data.

steps.title: 7 Distinguish between data problems and method problems
steps.body: Even if the data is clean, if the task itself cannot be solved through learning, it is a problem of method. For example, Gemini map tweaking is great for teaching niche formats or behaviors beyond what the base model already does well. The order is always data first, method second.

screens.outro: Now that you know the procedure, let's apply it to a real-world example.

screens.title: Case commentary: When data was improved by organizing it rather than increasing it
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case. Click the following button to compare the person in charge's initial response with the response after the audit.

steps.title: First Response: Double Your Data
steps.body: When the classification model's results faltered, staff doubled the examples. However, the same type of error continued. This is because if there are defects in the data, the more you increase the amount, the more of the same defects will be learned.

steps.title: What the Audit Reveals
steps.body: When I took a sample and checked it, I found that there were a bunch of different labels for the same input type, and there were many duplicate examples that were almost the same. The reason was that during the data collection process, several people used different labels to label the data.

steps.title: Result after cleanup
steps.body: By unifying the labeling criteria and removing duplicates, data decreased but model consistency increased. This is the principle that a small amount of high-quality data is more effective than a large amount of low-quality data.

steps.title: Target and supplement remaining weaknesses
steps.body: Even after cleaning up, one type was still weak, so I added an example targeting just that type. It was not increased blindly, but was added as needed after identifying weaknesses. When increasing the amount of data, you can gauge the benefit by comparing the results before and after the increase. There is also a way to see the gap by learning from the current data and the data halved.

steps.title: lesson
steps.body: If the results are shaky, do an audit before increasing the data. Cleaning up takes time, but it has the advantage of being smaller than the cost of restarting learning and being able to determine the cause. By recording the audit results and cleanup history, you can make sure that the same defect does not occur again in the next study. The audit is not done once; it is repeated each time data is added.

screens.outro: This time, we will look at a case where the problem was not resolved even after organizing the data.

screens.title: Case Commentary: When the problem was not the data but the method
screens.lead: The instructor explains and explains cases that cannot be solved even after organizing the data. Click the next button to follow the basis for your decision.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: We unified the labeling standards and removed duplicates, but the model does not consistently adhere to the standards. Now that all audit items have passed, it is no longer difficult to find data defects.

steps.title: Cause analysis
steps.body: Looking at the nature of the work again, it was not a matter of determining a single correct answer, but a comparison of preferences according to taste. Although there was a judgment as to which of the two responses was better, there was no single response that could be used as a standard.

steps.title: Select method
steps.body: An SFT that mimics a single baseline answer is not suitable for this task. That's right, DPO learns from pairs of good and bad responses. DPO is a format that provides a pair of preferred and non-preferred output for each prompt.

steps.title: What DPO data looks like
steps.body: The DPO training file is JSONL, with one line containing `input.messages`, `preferred_output`, and `non_preferred_output`. Both outputs must be the last assistant messages, and only learn one conversation turn. A preferred output is the ideal assistant response, and a non-preferred output is a less good response. For example, to the same question, answers with better tone and accuracy are placed on the preferred side, and vague answers are placed on the unpreferred side. DPOs are great for keeping your summary focused on important points or matching the tone and style of the conversation.

steps.title: Check before changing method
steps.body: Before changing your approach, check three things: First, did it pass all the items of the data audit? Second, did you first confirm the change with about 50 good examples? Third, were the before and after changes compared using the same evaluation criteria? This confirmation will provide a basis for your decision to change your approach.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: Only when things aren't resolved even after cleaning up the data do you change your method. By following this order, you can avoid waste where the same defects remain even after changing methods.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the inspection sequence so far at a glance.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of data quality diagnosis. Read slowly and think about what checks are needed on our data.

paragraphs: Data problems are divided into label mismatch, distribution bias, duplication, leakage, lack of evidence, and format mismatch. Label consistency sets the upper bound on model performance, distributions establish model habits, and redundancies and leaks inflate metrics and cloud judgment.

When the results are not as expected, the order is to start with a data audit, check samples, label, distribution, duplication and leakage, and format, and then target and supplement any remaining weaknesses. If it still doesn't work out, question the definition and method of the task.
Small amounts of high-quality data are more effective than large amounts of low-quality data. Therefore, it is efficient to check on the premise that most of the problems lie in the data.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: A high validation metric does not mean the data is good. This is because leaks and duplication can inflate metrics. Recording your audit results will help you review them more quickly in your next lesson.

checks.intro: Distinguish between types of data problems. Just choose the explanation that best fits the situation.
checks.q: 60% of responses for tuning are ‘can’t answer’, but in operations, that ratio should be around 5%. What problems are most likely to arise if we continue learning like this?
options: Evaluation data is mixed with learning, inflating indicators.
The same examples are repeated, resulting in overlearning of certain patterns.
Distribution bias causes the model to reject excessively
The information used in the response is missing from the input, so the model learns to make it up.
checks.explain: If the response distribution of the training data is significantly different from the distribution desired in operation, the model will learn the bias and reject it excessively.

wrong.0: This is a description of the leak and is different from the response rate issue.
wrong.1: This is an explanation of the duplication. The issue here is not repetition of examples, but proportion of response types.
wrong.3: This is an explanation without evidence. This is a different type of rejection rate problem.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. A distributional bias in which response rates are skewed leads to a model's rejection habits.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The type is out of sync. Pick again that the crux of the problem lies in the proportion of response types.

checks.intro: Think about the sequence of your data audit. Just arrange the items in the appropriate order.
checks.q: Lay out the order in which you would conduct your data audit
checks.explain: The flow starts with sample extraction, checks label matching, distribution, duplication, and leaks in order, and then unifies the format. Afterwards, any remaining weaknesses are supplemented with targeted examples.
checks.correctFeedback: The audit procedures have been arranged in the correct order.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. Try rearranging them so that reading the sample comes first and formatting comes last.

checks.intro: Consider the conclusion of the case commentary. You can use your judgment to choose the most appropriate one.
checks.q: Although the label standards have been unified and duplicates have been removed, the model cannot consistently adhere to the standards because the standard is not a single standard answer but rather a comparison of preferences based on taste. How to judge correctly?
options: Consider changing the method to a DPO that learns from pairs of good and bad responses.
Double the number of SFT examples that mimic one standard answer
Since it is not a data problem, throw away all the training data and recreate it.
Increase consistency by increasing the ratio of verification data
checks.explain: If it is not resolved even after organizing the data and the essence is preference comparison, it is a method issue. DPO is suited to this task by providing pairs of preferred and non-preferred responses.

wrong.1: In tasks where there is more than one standard answer, simply increasing examples repeats the same limitations.
wrong.2: There is no reason to throw away data that has already been organized, and the reason is that the method is not suitable.
wrong.3: Validation rate is independent of whether the learning method is suitable for the task.

checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. Even after organizing the data, we followed the order of changing the method when it was not resolved.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Note that the data cleaning has already been completed. Think again about what the remaining causes are in this case.

glossary.def: The same type of input is labeled with different criteria. Lower the upper limit on model performance.
The type ratio of the training data is different from the operational input and is lopsided.
This is a phenomenon where evaluation data is mixed with learning and the indicators appear better than they actually are.
The same or almost the same examples are repeated.
This is a procedure to systematically check for data problems through sampling and aggregation.

misconceptions.myth: If the results are bad, just collect more data.
misconceptions.fact: If your data has flaws, the same errors will increase as you increase the amount. First, we audit to find defects.

misconceptions.myth: If tuning gets worse, it's the hyperparameters' fault.
misconceptions.fact: It is efficient to first check the consistency and distribution of data before changing settings.

misconceptions.myth: If the validation index is high, the data is okay.
misconceptions.fact: Leaks and duplications can inflate metrics. Don't assume your data is healthy just because of high metrics.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Much of the problem lies in the data.
Label consistency sets the upper bound on model performance.
Distribution, duplication, leaks, and absence of evidence are audit items.
When cleaning up the data doesn't work, you question the method.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If we were to check our data, what would we check first and why?
